prompt: News organisations sometimes publish stories that later turn out to be false. Some people believe that the law should require corrections to be given the same prominence as the original story. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
News organisations make mistakes, and a false story can do lasting damage long before anyone establishes that it was false. I broadly agree that corrections should be legally required to match the prominence of the original report, although I would limit the requirement to stories that caused identifiable harm.

The argument in favour is essentially about reach. A story printed on a front page or pushed to millions of phones is seen by an audience that a paragraph on an inside page will never reach, so a correction published quietly does not undo the error; it merely allows the publisher to claim that it has been undone. Where a false report has damaged a person's reputation or a company's trade, leaving the scale of the remedy to the publisher's discretion is unlikely to produce a fair result, because the publisher has an obvious interest in keeping the admission small.

The objection is that a rigid rule would be costly to apply. Newsrooms produce a great deal of material and much of it contains small inaccuracies, a misspelled name or a wrong figure, that nobody would seriously want on the front page. A law drafted without a threshold would either be ignored or would push editors towards caution, which is not the same as accuracy. This is an argument for defining harm carefully, though, rather than for leaving the matter to the industry.

My view is therefore that the requirement should exist but should be triggered by consequence rather than by error. Where a false story has measurably harmed someone, the correction should be as loud as the accusation. Where it has not, ordinary editorial judgement is enough, and the law has no business intervening.
title: Making corrections as prominent as the story
